title: Ethernet Frames: The Complete Beginner's Guide

scenes.narration: Before data crosses a cable, it goes into an envelope. It has addresses on the front, and a check on the back. That's an Ethernet frame.

lines.t: Your data goes in an envelope

scenes.heading: The postal envelope
scenes.narration: The letter inside is your I P packet. The envelope has a return address, which is the source M A C. It has a destination address, the destination M A C. And a little note saying what's inside, which is the EtherType. At the end, the post office adds a seal, called the F C S, so the receiver can check nothing was damaged. If the seal doesn't match, the frame is thrown away.

scenes.heading: Sizes to know
scenes.narration: Three numbers matter. The smallest frame is sixty-four bytes. The biggest standard payload is fifteen hundred. And the header is fourteen bytes, with a four byte trailer.

scenes.heading: Common mix-ups
scenes.narration: Three slip-ups. The preamble and S F D aren't counted in the frame size. The minimum payload is forty-six bytes, not sixty-four. And in Ethernet two, the EtherType says what's inside, not how long it is.

items.wrong: The preamble counts in the frame size
items.right: It's physical layer overhead, not counted
In Ethernet II it's a protocol type

scenes.heading: Remember this
scenes.cta: Try the Courseiva Ethernet frames lab
scenes.narration: So, to recap. A frame has addresses, a type, the data and a check. Minimum is sixty-four bytes, and maximum payload is fifteen hundred. A bad F C S means the frame is dropped. Ready to practise? Try the Courseiva Ethernet frames lab.
